topic.title: We read the EMI, not the loan
topic.claim: We'll compare two apps for twenty minutes over ₹40, then sign a home loan where a longer tenure quietly adds lakhs.
topic.moment: The bank says 'we can bring the EMI down if we stretch it to 25 years' and everyone at the table relaxes.

turn.believed: A lower EMI means the loan got cheaper.
turn.actually: A longer tenure usually means far more interest overall, and the bank earns more from it.

topic.because: We feel the EMI every month, but the total interest is a number we never see on one screen. Banks sell the comfortable monthly figure.
topic.payoff: Before you sign, ask for the total you'll pay over the full loan. Then decide if the low EMI still feels good.
topic.behaviour: Buyers pick longer tenures to fit EMIs; banks offer tenure stretches as a favour.
topic.mechanism: Monthly comfort hides the total cost, which is where the bank earns.
topic.group: First-time home buyers, late 20s to early 30s
topic.send_to: The couple in your life who is about to book their first flat.
topic.why_now: With flats costing a decade or more of salary, longer loans are becoming the default.

score.why: We compare apps over ₹40 and then take the low EMI of a longer loan. It's a dark pattern with a test the reader can run before signing.

topic.villain: a loan-tenure structure that hides the total interest behind a low EMI

notes: Slide 1 promises 'haggle over small change, then sign away lakhs' but the carousel never shows the small-change haggling side of that contrast - it jumps straight to the loan desk. Add a beat (even one line) showing the reader nitpicking something small elsewhere so the headline's irony actually pays off by slide 6.

Slide 5: 'Nobody at the table adds up what the comfort costs across all those years. The monthly figure is the only one they show you.' iq is borderline - 'longer tenure means more total interest' is common financial knowledge, so the insight lands softer than it could. Slide 6's payoff ('ask for one number... Read it out loud at the table') leans close to an instruction/checkout-rule. It's allowed as a test, but consider phrasing it as something the reader does in the moment rather than a directive, so it stings rather than lectures.

Old news framed as new: 'At the loan desk, the monthly EMI figure is displayed but the total amount that will be repaid over the full loan tenure is not shown.' (first reported 2024-10-01). Frame it as past, or drop it. What's true: Since 1 October 2024, RBI's Key Facts Statement (KFS) mandate requires all regulated lenders to disclose the 'Total Interest Amount' and the 'Total amount to be paid by the borrower' (sanctioned amount + total interest) over the full tenor, plus an amortisation schedule, before the loan agreement is signed — for all new retail (including home) and MSME term loans. The claim that total repayment is not shown was true before this rule but is no longer generally true..

mechanism.actual_mechanism: A home-loan EMI is a fixed amortizing payment covering interest on the outstanding balance plus principal. At a given rate, lengthening the tenure shrinks the share of each EMI that pays down principal, so the balance falls more slowly and interest accrues on a larger balance for more months. The monthly figure drops, but the sum of all EMIs (principal + total interest) rises — e.g. ₹40L at 8.5% over 20 years repays ~₹83L, ~₹43L of it interest, and stretching to 25 years lowers the EMI while pushing total interest higher.

sources.quote: When the tenure is longer, an even bigger portion of the EMI goes towards interest payment and less towards principal payment.
A longer tenure reduces monthly EMI, [but] it increases the overall interest payment.

ledger.text: A home loan's tenure can be stretched to twenty-five years as a way to lower the EMI.
Stretching a home loan's tenure lowers the monthly EMI but increases the total amount repaid, because the extra years add more cumulative interest, and that added interest is what the bank earns.
ledger.sentence: The monthly figure gets smaller. The total you pay back gets bigger, because every extra year adds more interest. Those extra years aren't a kindness. They're where the bank earns.

sources.quote: 25 years is the maximum Home Loan tenure you can choose at HDFC Bank... For a ₹45 Lakh loan at 8% interest: 20 years: ₹36,943 EMI; 25 years: ₹33,990 EMI

Borrowers have a choice: absorb interest rate increases through a higher EMI or keep the EMI unchanged and extend the loan tenure... For a ₹40 lakh home loan at 7.5% for 25 years, the EMI is about ₹29,559

mechanism.actual_mechanism: A home loan amortizes: each EMI covers the month's interest on the outstanding balance plus some principal. Lengthening the tenure shrinks the principal portion per installment, so the balance falls more slowly and accrues interest over more months — the EMI drops but total interest rises. That interest is precisely the lender's income on the loan, so the extra years do add to what the bank earns. Concrete check at ~8.5% on ₹50 lakh: ~20-year total interest ≈ ₹54 lakh vs ~25-year ≈ ₹71 lakh, a ~₹17 lakh increase for a monthly saving of only ~₹2,500.

sources.quote: If the tenure is longer, an even bigger portion of the EMI goes towards interest payment and less towards principal payment. Hence, the principal goes down slowly.
Longer home loan tenure reduces EMI but increases interest cost.
For a ₹50 Lakh loan at 8.50%: 20 Years costs ₹54.14 Lakh in total interest, while 25 Years costs ₹70.78 Lakh.

_ledger.text:
[cover] You'll haggle over small change, then sign away [lakhs for a lower EMI]
The bank stretches the tenure like it's doing you a favour.
 

[slide 1] You'll haggle over small change, then sign away lakhs for a lower EMI.
Swipe to read →

[slide 2] You're at the loan desk, both your names on the same form. A pen that isn't yours, cold in your hand.
The EMI they first quote lands like a weight on your chest.

[slide 3] You go quiet. They see it. 'We can bring this down,' they say. 'Stretch it to twenty-five years.'
The number drops. Your shoulders drop with it. Everyone at the table breathes out.

[slide 4] They offered it like a favour, and relief feels like good news. So nobody runs the other sum.
The monthly figure gets smaller. The total you pay back gets bigger, because every extra year adds more interest.
Those extra years aren't a kindness. They're where the bank earns.

[slide 5] And a lower EMI does help. It fits the salary, leaves room for groceries and the metro card. That part is real.
So you tell each other the rest will sort itself out. 'We'll prepay once the raises come.' 'The flat's value will cover it anyway.'
Most of that never happens.

[slide 6] Before you nod, ask for one number out loud: the full amount you'll have paid by the last EMI.
That's the figure that should land on your chest, not the monthly one.
The weight you felt first was the honest number. The relief was sold to you.

[end card] Open this again the evening before you meet the loan officer.
Send to the couple who just shortlisted their first flat and keep repeating the EMI like it's the whole price.

The post tells readers to ask for the full amount they will pay over the whole loan before signing.
